title: Slav Defense: the bishop-out plan and the recapture
outcomes: Is shown the Slav Defense by its first moves (1.d4 d5 2.c4 c6) and what c6 does that e6 does not: it guards d5 and leaves the c8 bishop's diagonal open
Decides whether ...Bf5 is playable by checking which white pawn or piece attacks f5, not by habit
As White, regains the c4 pawn with the f1 bishop once e3 is played, and checks what the opponent's last move attacks before developing
Is shown opening statistics as results of games with a stated source and sample size, not as evaluations

steps.text: **Slav Defense** (ECO D10, the standard code): 1.d4 d5 2.c4 c6. In our online data (4,752,291 games, September 2026, all rating bands) 48,185 games reach this position. Among masters (329,379 games, both players rated 2500 or more) Black chose 2...c6 in 9,705 games and 2...e6 in 9,585. The c6 pawn guards d5, as e6 would, but unlike e6 it leaves the c8 bishop's diagonal to h3 open. The board shows one main line.

steps.caption: Position after 1.d4 d5 2.c4, Black to move. Step through one main line (our opening data names it the Three Knights Variation, and after 4...dxc4 the Two Knights Attack). Other moves are possible.

line.say: c6 guards d5 with a pawn and leaves the c8 bishop's diagonal open.
Nf3 develops a knight and guards d4.
Nf6 develops a knight and also guards d5.
dxc4 takes the pawn on c4. Black is a pawn up for now.
a4 stops ...b5, which would defend the extra pawn.
Bf5 puts the bishop outside the pawn chain, before ...e6 closes it in.
e3 opens the diagonal of the f1 bishop to c4.
e6 closes the centre behind the bishop and opens the f8 bishop.
Bb4 attacks the knight on c3.

claims.statement: After ...c6 exactly one black pawn (c6) attacks d5, so it guards d5.
After ...c6 the bishop on c8 attacks along the diagonal through f5, g4 and h3.
Had Black played ...e6 instead, the bishop on c8 would not attack f5, g4 or h3.
After dxc4 the black pawn stands on c4.
After a4 the pawn attacks b5.
After ...Bf5 the bishop attacks e4, d3 and c2.
After ...e6 the bishop on f8 attacks along the diagonal through e7, d6, c5 and b4.
After Bxc4 the white bishop stands on c4.

steps.text: **What strong players chose** (results of games, not evaluations). Source: masters data, 329,379 games, both players rated 2500 or more. After 1.d4 d5 2.c4 c6 3.Nf3 Nf6 4.Nc3 (any move order), Black played ...e6 in 2,227 games (White won 693, 1,036 drawn, Black won 498) and ...dxc4 in 1,742 (554, 852, 336). After 4...dxc4, which 1,759 games reached (a few by other move orders), White played 5.a4 in 1,517. Samples are small; results also reflect the players.

**Black's side (rule of thumb).** Black develops the c8 bishop outside the pawn chain, with ...Bf5 or ...Bg4, before closing it in with ...e6. Condition: the square must be safe. After 5.a4 it is; after 5.e4 a pawn attacks f5. Before you move a bishop out, ask: which white pawn or piece attacks the square I am going to? The next step tests this.

steps.title: One pawn moves, the bishop plan flips
steps.prompt: In all three positions Black considers ...Bf5. Predict for each whether it is reasonable, then check. The first two differ only in White's fifth move (a4 or e4). The third differs from the first only in where White's h-pawn stands (h3 or h2).

steps.text: **White's side (rule of thumb).** After ...dxc4 White usually regains the pawn with the f1 bishop once e3 has opened its diagonal, then may build pawns on d4 and e4. Condition: every move must still pass the question, what does my opponent's last move attack? The next two items: first regain the pawn, then pick a central move, where one natural-looking developing move is rated at least a pawn worse.

steps.prompt: Think about the positions you played without hints. Before you chose a move, what did you check? Write one line for each side.

fields.label: As Black: what I checked before moving the bishop or closing the centre
As White: what I checked before developing a piece
